archetype.name: Better Than Its Record (pass-first)
archetype.definition: A team whose efficient Stroud-led passing game and positive point differential point to a winning club, but whose 4-6 record has been dragged down by a string of one-score losses, a dead run game and leaky big-play defense.

report.headline: A winning team's profile stuck inside a losing record; the close losses should even out.
report.take:
These Texans have flipped identities. Last year's 12-5 team won with the league's second-best defense by EPA and a 22nd-ranked offense. This year the offense carries the team: eighth in EPA per play, ninth in points at 26.1 a game, driven by C.J. Stroud throwing behind a line that allows the fourth-lowest pressure rate in the league. The defense has slipped to the middle of the pack at 17th in EPA allowed. It still leads the league in sacks, but it no longer suffocates people.

The record misreads the team. Houston has outscored opponents by 37 points, a margin worth 5.8 wins, not four, and its -1.82 wins over expected ranks 30th. Every loss has come by six points or fewer: Buffalo, Cincinnati aside, Indianapolis by two, Dallas by four, the Giants and Cleveland late. The wins have mostly been routs: 26-3 twice, 44-22 at the Chargers. A 0.2 one-score win rate is not a skill this team lacks so much as a coin that keeps landing tails, and it usually doesn't keep doing that.

What the numbers hide is where the close games are being lost. The run game is a liability: 3.32 yards a carry (28th) and 2.16 yards before contact (27th), so the line that protects Stroud so well cannot move anyone, and the offense can't close games on the ground or convert short yardage (25th). On defense, Houston wins downs (seventh in success rate allowed) but gives up explosive passes at the second-worst rate in the league and scores touchdowns in the red zone 22nd-best. Add 679 penalty yards, 21st-ranked special teams and a conservative fourth-down approach (29th in go rate), and you get a good team that hands back margin in small, fixable ways.

The direction is encouraging. After a sluggish September in which the pass offense posted negative EPA in two of the first three games, Stroud has put up big passing days against Dallas, Jacksonville, Tennessee and the Chargers, and the defense just held Indianapolis to 38 rushing yards. The problem is the calendar: Jacksonville sits at 7-3 atop the division, so the realistic path is a wild card, and the stretch after Baltimore is the hardest part of the schedule.

strengths.title: Stroud's passing behind elite protection
strengths.body: Houston ranks eighth in pass EPA, and it starts with the line: only three teams allow a lower pressure rate, and the QB hit rate allowed is fifth-lowest. Stroud gets clean pockets, and the offense passes a bit more than expected because of it. This has held all season and should hold, provided Rutledge's stinger and Teller's back don't thin the interior.

strengths.title: League-leading pass rush
strengths.body: The defense leads the league in sacks and ranks third in sack rate, and that pressure is a big reason it ranks seventh in success rate allowed. It's real and repeatable, but Danielle Hunter's hamstring and Rankins' ankle test how much of it survives on the injury report.

strengths.title: Point differential says winning team
strengths.body: A +37 differential implies 5.8 wins against an actual four, and the blowout wins over Tennessee, the Chargers and Indianapolis show the ceiling. Differential predicts future records better than record does, which makes Houston a better bet than 4-6 suggests.

concerns.title: A run game that can't close
concerns.body: Houston runs for 3.32 yards a carry with a 33.7% success rate, near the bottom of the league, and the blocking is the cause, not the backs: defenders are meeting runners barely two yards past the line. That makes it hard to protect leads or convert short yardage, which matters in the one-score games this team keeps losing. With Teller out and Rutledge questionable, a quick fix is unlikely.

concerns.title: Big plays allowed through the air
concerns.body: The defense wins most downs but gives up explosive passes at the 31st-ranked rate and grades poorly on deep throws, and opponents' second receivers have done real damage. It's the cost of an aggressive front: when the rush doesn't get home, the back end gets stretched. It explains why a top-seven success-rate defense allows 24 points a game.

concerns.title: Self-inflicted margin leaks
concerns.body: Penalties (23rd per game), special teams (21st) and a 22nd-ranked red-zone defense keep turning wins into coin flips; 112 penalty yards in the three-point loss at Cleveland is the clearest example. These are discipline and coaching items, so they can improve, but they've persisted all year.

trend.note: The pass offense sputtered in September (negative EPA against Cincinnati and Indianapolis) and has been mostly strong since, peaking with 391 passing yards at the Chargers. The results still swing week to week because the close games keep breaking the wrong way.

nextGame.headline: Stroud's passing game meets a Ravens secondary missing pieces
nextGame.body:
Houston is a 6.5-point home favorite (-310) against a Ravens team at 4-7 that has been outscored on the season and is now playing without Lamar Jackson, who is on injured reserve after thumb surgery. Baltimore has cycled through Huntley, Fagnano and Brissett, and its offense ranks 19th in EPA with a line that allows the fourth-highest pressure rate. The matchup that matters most is Houston's pass game against a defense that ranks 30th on deep passes and 31st against opposing WR1s. Baltimore's identity is the ground game (4.4 yards a carry, seventh) and an always-go fourth-down approach.

Availability cuts both ways. Baltimore is without Madubuike up front, safety Jaylinn Hawkins, and likely corner Marlon Humphrey, which thins exactly the secondary Houston wants to attack. Houston is missing Danielle Hunter and may be without Rankins, which weakens the rush against a vulnerable line and the run defense against Baltimore's best weapon. Woody Marks (concussion) is trending toward playing; if not, David Montgomery takes the carries. Marvin Harrison Jr. is out, Boutte is questionable, and Rutledge's stinger is worth watching on a line already missing Teller. Houston comes in with ten days of rest after the Thursday win.

waysToWin.title: Nico Collins over a thin secondary
waysToWin.body: Baltimore allows 0.72 EPA per target to opposing WR1s, 31st in the league, and ranks 30th on deep passes, now without Hawkins and probably Humphrey. Collins leads Houston in targets, and Stroud's clean pockets give him time to push the ball downfield. A few explosives here likely decide the game.

waysToWin.title: Pressure a backup QB into mistakes
waysToWin.body: Even without Hunter, Houston's pass rush faces a line that allows the fourth-highest pressure rate and a 24th-ranked sack rate, with a backup quarterback behind it. Getting Baltimore into obvious passing downs and turning sacks into stalled drives is how the Texans held Indianapolis and Tennessee to three points.

waysToWin.title: Win the hidden yardage
waysToWin.body: Baltimore's special teams rank 27th and it commits penalties even more often than Houston. If the Texans simply play clean, the field-position edge that has cost them close games can swing their way for once.

waysToLose.title: Baltimore runs through a depleted front
waysToLose.body: Baltimore's one reliable weapon is a run game at 4.4 yards a carry, and Houston ranks 20th in rushing yards allowed with Hunter out and Rankins questionable. The Giants ran for 188 in the upset here. If the Ravens can lean on the ground and go for it on every fourth down, they shorten the game and keep it close.

waysToLose.title: Another one-score game handed away
waysToLose.body: Houston has lost its close games all season, and the giveaways are familiar: penalties, red-zone touchdowns allowed, and a run game that can't finish drives. A sluggish start against a big underdog, like the NYG loss as a 10-point favorite, turns this into the kind of game Houston keeps losing.

waysToLose.title: Explosive passes from a backup
waysToLose.body: Houston's back end gives up big plays at the 31st-ranked rate. Even a backup quarterback can steal a game with two or three chunk plays when the rush doesn't get home, and that rush is missing its best edge player.

nextGame.watch: Houston's early downfield shots to Collins: if Baltimore's patched secondary gives up an explosive or two in the first half, the Ravens' backup-led offense isn't built to chase.

restOfSeason.body:
The efficiency is real and the record should catch up, at least partly. A top-ten pass offense behind elite protection and a top-ranked pass rush is a sustainable core, and one-score luck this bad tends to regress toward even. What won't change quickly is the run blocking and the big-play leaks, which put a ceiling on how dominant this team can be and keep close games likely.

The schedule is the problem. After Baltimore come road trips to Pittsburgh (8th-ranked defense), Washington and Green Bay, a home date with 7-3 Jacksonville (second-ranked defense) and a soft finish against Philadelphia and Tennessee. Catching Jacksonville in the division is a long shot; the realistic goal is a wild card, which probably requires winning this week and stealing at least one of the tough road games. Expect points to dip a bit against the stronger defenses ahead.
swingFactors: Danielle Hunter's return from the hamstring
Interior line health (Rutledge, Teller) for the run game

confidence.note: Ten games; efficiency and differential agree, but close-game outcomes and injuries add noise.
